notes: Batch 2 (40 species), prepared by the coding agent on 2026-11-22 at the owner's request, for a portfolio project. Sources read that day: GBIF Backbone Taxonomy (CC BY 4.0) via the GBIF API for names and classification; Wikidata (CC0) for the IUCN category, cited second-hand with the IUCN edition its statement references; English Wikipedia (one revision per species, recorded in each source) for range countries and seas, habitats, diet, threats and population figures, restated in our own words. IUCN pages were not read. Habitat and threat codes are our own lists (w-*), not the IUCN schemes. Countries and seas are those the article names; many lists are partial and say so in the geography citation note. Images from Wikimedia Commons, downloaded into catalogue/media: licence read from the Commons API at download time and compared with the file's embedded copyright fields; files without a named creator were not used. Trend is 'unknown' throughout.

editorial.overview: The largest land animal in Asia and the only living species of its genus. It has one finger-like tip on its trunk, small ears, and tusks mostly in males. Herds of females and calves move together, while adult males live alone or in loose groups. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A plant eater that both grazes and browses, eating up to 150 kg of plants a day from more than a hundred plant species, with more bark in the dry season. It drinks at least once a day and stays close to fresh water.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Global wild population estimate for 2019.

citations.note: Range from India to Borneo and Sumatra; the countries listed are those the article names for wild elephants. Bhutan is not named in this revision.

media.altText: An Asian elephant in grassland

editorial.overview: The smallest living rhinoceros and the only one with a hairy coat. Like the African species it has two horns. It once lived across mainland Southeast Asia and now survives only in a few small populations on Sumatra and Borneo. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Browses young saplings, leaves, twigs and shoots, up to about 50 kg a day, from more than a hundred plant species. It feeds mostly in the morning and just before nightfall.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Stated as fewer than 80 mature individuals in five populations.

citations.note: Wild populations on Sumatra and in East Kalimantan (Borneo), Indonesia. Extirpated in Malaysia in 2019.

media.altText: A Sumatran rhinoceros mother with her calf

editorial.overview: A great ape of the forests and savannas of equatorial Africa and, with the bonobo, the closest living relative of humans. Chimpanzees live in communities that can exceed 200 members and use tools. Four subspecies are recognised. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mostly ripe fruit, plus leaves, seeds, flowers, pith, bark and resin. It also eats honey, insects, eggs and small to medium-sized mammals, including other primates.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Wild population across the range.

citations.note: Countries named in the article for the four subspecies.

media.altText: An adult male chimpanzee sitting in forest

editorial.overview: The smallest great ape, found only south of the Congo River. Bonobos are more slender than chimpanzees, with a dark face, pink lips and long parted hair. Their groups are led largely by bonded females. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly fruit (more than half the diet), with leaves, honey, eggs, invertebrates and small mammals such as duikers and flying squirrels.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Conservative estimate; no precise count exists.

citations.note: Humid forests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, between the Congo and Kasai rivers.

media.altText: Bonobos grooming each other in a tree

editorial.overview: A medium-sized lemur, the best known of all, recognised by its long black-and-white ringed tail. It lives in groups and spends more time on the ground than other lemurs. It is found only in southern and south-western Madagascar. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An opportunistic omnivore that eats mainly fruit and leaves, especially of the tamarind tree, which can make up half its diet in the dry season. It also eats flowers, herbs, bark and sap.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Stated as "as few as 2,000" in the wild in early 2017. Approximate.

citations.note: Endemic to southern and south-western Madagascar.

media.altText: A ring-tailed lemur on a branch

editorial.overview: The longest member of the weasel family, reaching about 1.8 m. Unlike most otters it is social, living in family groups that hunt and defend territory together. It has lost much of its South American range. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An apex predator of rivers that feeds mainly on fish such as cichlids, perch, characins (including piranha) and catfish.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Wild population estimates are "typically below 5,000".

citations.note: The range countries the article lists; French Guiana is also listed but is not a separate region in our map. Range is now patchy after local extinctions.

media.altText: A giant otter eating a fish in a river

editorial.overview: A slender, reddish wolf of the Ethiopian Highlands and the rarest canid in the world. It lives in packs but hunts alone, mostly for rodents. It survives in a few isolated mountain ranges. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly big-headed African mole-rats in the Bale Mountains, plus grass rats, other rodents and highland hares; occasionally goslings, eggs, rock hyraxes and young antelope.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Adult population in 2011, more than half of it in the Bale Mountains.

citations.note: Afroalpine grassland and heath of the Ethiopian Highlands, mostly above 3,000 m.

media.altText: An Ethiopian wolf standing in highland grass

editorial.overview: The largest wild dog in Africa, with a mottled coat of black, yellow and white. It lives and hunts in packs, chasing prey over long distances. It has disappeared from much of North and West Africa. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A pack hunter of medium-sized antelope, which it runs down in long chases at up to 66 km/h.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: An estimated 6,600 adults, of which about 1,400 are mature individuals, in 39 subpopulations.

citations.note: Partial list: countries the article names for current populations (South Africa via Kruger National Park). Occasional sightings in Guinea and Mali are not listed.

media.altText: An African wild dog resting

editorial.overview: A scaly, toothless mammal of Southeast Asia that rolls into a ball when threatened. Its name comes from the Malay word for "roller". Like all pangolins it is heavily poached and trafficked. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Ants and termites, which it collects with a long, sticky tongue.

population.note: No population figure in the source.

citations.note: Countries named in the article (Indonesia for Borneo, Java, Sumatra and the Lesser Sunda Islands). Singapore is also named but is too small for our map.

media.altText: A Sunda pangolin climbing over branches at night

editorial.overview: A tree-living monkey of Borneo, named for the very large nose of adult males. It lives near coasts and rivers and is a good swimmer. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly young leaves and unripe fruit, from at least 55 plant species, plus some flowers, seeds and insects. It eats more fruit early in the year and more leaves later.

population.note: No total in the source; it says the population fell by more than 50% in the 36–40 years to 2008.

citations.note: Endemic to Borneo, in all three countries that share the island.

media.altText: A male proboscis monkey in a tree

editorial.overview: A large, muscular cat and the only cat that lives in groups, called prides. Males usually carry a mane. Today it lives only in scattered populations in sub-Saharan Africa and, as the Asiatic lion, around Gir National Park in India. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An apex predator of medium to large hoofed mammals such as wildebeest, zebra, buffalo, gemsbok and giraffe, and often warthog. In India it mostly takes chital and sambar deer.

population.note: No global count in the source. It says African populations fell by about 43% since the early 1990s.

citations.note: Partial list: countries where the article places a current population (for example Gir in India, Serengeti in Tanzania, Chobe in Botswana, Waza in Cameroon, and the W–Arly–Pendjari parks of Benin, Burkina Faso and Niger).

media.altText: A male lion lying in the grass of the Masai Mara

editorial.overview: The heaviest member of the weasel family and one of the smallest marine mammals. It has the densest fur of any animal instead of blubber. Hunting for fur almost wiped it out; it has since returned to about two-thirds of its old range on North Pacific coasts. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Eats at least a fifth of its body weight a day, mainly sea urchins and other invertebrates of the sea floor, which it often opens with stones while floating. By eating urchins it protects kelp forests.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Russian coasts only (Kuril Islands, Kamchatka, Commander Islands), about 27,000 in 2004. No global total in the source.

citations.note: Coasts of the North Pacific from northern Japan and Russia to Alaska, British Columbia, California and Mexico.

media.altText: A sea otter floating on its back in a harbour

editorial.overview: A large baleen whale, slow and docile, that floats when dead, which made it the "right" whale to hunt. Whaling left very few. The western population migrates between feeding grounds off New England and Canada and calving grounds off Georgia and Florida. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Skims slowly through dense patches of copepods and other small invertebrates such as krill and larval barnacles, at or below the surface.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Stated as about 380 individuals, including about 70 breeding females, "as of 2026".

citations.note: Coastal waters of the western North Atlantic, from Florida to Canada. The eastern population may be functionally extinct.

media.altText: A North Atlantic right whale and her calf seen from above

editorial.overview: A shy forest relative of the giraffe, with a dark body and zebra-like stripes on its legs. It lives only in the rainforests of the north-east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Browses leaves and buds of understory plants, plus grasses, ferns, fruit and fungi, using a long tongue to pick suitable plants.

population.note: No total in the source; it reports a steady decline.

citations.note: Endemic to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, mainly north and east of the Congo River (Ituri forest, Okapi Wildlife Reserve, Maiko National Park).

media.altText: An okapi in a forest enclosure

editorial.overview: The largest living carnivorous marsupial, about the size of a small dog, with a powerful bite and a loud screech. It died out on mainland Australia about 3,500 years ago and now lives only on Tasmania, where a contagious facial cancer has cut its numbers. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An opportunist that eats carrion more often than live prey. It favours wombats and eats small mammals such as wallabies, as well as birds, fish, insects and some fruit.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Tasmanian government calculation for 2008: 10,000 to 100,000 individuals, with 20,000 to 50,000 mature individuals likely.

citations.note: Island of Tasmania, Australia. Extinct on the mainland for about 3,500 years.

media.altText: A Tasmanian devil

editorial.overview: A huge, barrel-shaped mammal of sub-Saharan Africa that spends the day in rivers and lakes and comes out at night to graze. Its closest living relatives are whales and dolphins. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A grazer: it stays in water or mud by day and leaves at dusk to eat grass, usually feeding alone.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Stable population as reported for 2017.

citations.note: Partial list: countries named in the ranges of the subspecies (from Gambia east to Ethiopia, south to South Africa, Angola and Namibia).

media.altText: A hippopotamus in the water

editorial.overview: The largest river dolphin, often pink in adults, found only in the Amazon and Orinoco basins of South America. In the rainy season it swims out of the main rivers into flooded forest. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: The most varied diet of any toothed whale: at least 53 species of fish, mostly croakers, cichlids, characins and piranhas, usually 5 to 80 cm long.

citations.note: The six South American countries the article lists, in the Amazon and Orinoco river systems.

media.altText: An Amazon river dolphin under water

editorial.overview: A tall, grey wading bird of central African swamps, named for its enormous shoe-shaped bill. Adults are mainly grey. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mostly fish, especially lungfish, bichirs, tilapia and catfish, plus frogs, water snakes and other wetland animals.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Estimate as given in the source.

citations.note: Freshwater swamps from South Sudan (the Sudd) and southern Sudan through Uganda, eastern DR Congo and Rwanda to western Tanzania and northern Zambia.

media.altText: A shoebill taking off over a lake

editorial.overview: A large, olive-green parrot of the mountains of New Zealand's South Island, with orange under its wings. It is one of the few parrots that live above the tree line and is known for its intelligence and curiosity. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An omnivore: more than 40 plant species, beetle larvae, grasshoppers, snails, seabird chicks and carrion.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Estimates published in 2017.

citations.note: Endemic to the South Island of New Zealand, from western lowland valleys up to alpine areas.

media.altText: A kea perched on a rock

editorial.overview: The longest parrot in the world, about one metre from head to tail, blue with a yellow ring around the eye and yellow skin under the beak. It lives in central and eastern South America, mainly the Pantanal and the cerrado. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly nuts of particular palms, such as acuri and bocaiuva, plus fruit. Its powerful beak can crack very hard nuts.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: World Wildlife Fund figure for 2004, as cited in the article. Approximate.

citations.note: The Pantanal of Brazil with nearby eastern Bolivia and north-eastern Paraguay, the cerrado of eastern Brazil, and open areas along south-eastern Amazon rivers.

media.altText: A hyacinth macaw in a tree with pink blossoms

editorial.overview: A very large dark eagle with white shoulders, white tail and a large yellow beak; it is usually the heaviest eagle in the world. It breeds in the Russian Far East and many birds winter in Japan. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly fish, especially Pacific salmon and trout such as pink and chum salmon, as an apex predator of its rivers and coasts.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Stated as "estimated at 5,000 and decreasing". Approximate.

citations.note: Breeds on Kamchatka, around the Sea of Okhotsk, on the lower Amur and northern Sakhalin (Russia); winters south to Hokkaido and the southern Kurils, Korea and China. Korea is not shown, because the source does not say which part of the peninsula.

media.altText: A Steller's sea eagle holding a fish

editorial.overview: A very large hornbill with a solid, ivory-like casque on its bill, which makes up about a tenth of its weight. Males ram each other with their casques in flight. Poaching for this "hornbill ivory" drove it to Critically Endangered. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mostly the fruit of strangler figs.

population.note: No global total in the source; it says fewer than 100 birds remain in Thai forests.

citations.note: The Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Borneo, Thailand and Myanmar, as named in the article.

media.altText: A helmeted hornbill on a branch

editorial.overview: A glossy black ibis with a bare red face and head, 70 to 80 cm long. Unlike most ibises it nests on cliff ledges and feeds in dry country. It vanished from Europe over 300 years ago; the main wild population is now in southern Morocco. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Lizards, insects and other small animals, caught in flocks on dry steppe, fallow fields and grazed land near the breeding cliffs.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: About 700 wild birds in southern Morocco in 2019. Captive and reintroduced birds are not counted.

citations.note: Wild breeding colonies at Souss-Massa and nearby in southern Morocco. A semi-wild colony at Birecik, Turkey, and reintroduction sites in Austria, Italy and Spain.

media.altText: A northern bald ibis

editorial.overview: The only penguin that breeds in Africa, found on the coasts and islands of South Africa and Namibia. Once numbering in the millions, it is now the rarest penguin species. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List, as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Forages in the open sea for small schooling fish such as sardines and anchovies, plus squid and small crustaceans like krill.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: About 19,800 mature individuals as of 2024, declining.

citations.note: Colonies on about two dozen islands and a few mainland sites between Namibia and Algoa Bay, South Africa.

media.altText: An African penguin on a beach

editorial.overview: A tortoise of southern Madagascar with a high-domed shell marked by bright yellow lines radiating from the centre of each plate. It is heavily collected for food and the pet trade. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly grazes on grasses and other plants, which make up 80 to 90% of its diet, plus fruit and succulent plants.

population.note: No estimates of the wild population are available; numbers are declining.

citations.note: Native to the far south and south-west of Madagascar. Introduced to Réunion and Mauritius, which are too small for our map.

media.altText: A radiated tortoise

editorial.overview: A small alligator, one of only two living alligator species, once found throughout the Yangtze river system. In the wild it now survives only in a few ponds and wetlands in southern Anhui province, China, and it is among the most endangered crocodilians. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An opportunistic carnivore that eats mostly fish and invertebrates such as snails, clams, mussels, crustaceans and insects, and sometimes rodents and water birds.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Total wild population estimated from a 2015 survey (68–86 adults).

citations.note: Small ponds and wetlands in south-eastern Anhui province, China.

media.altText: A Chinese alligator resting

editorial.overview: A sea turtle with a large head and powerful jaws, found in the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian oceans and the Mediterranean. It nests over a wider range than any other sea turtle; hatchlings drift in floating sargassum before moving to coastal waters. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An omnivore that mainly eats bottom-dwelling invertebrates such as whelks, conchs, clams and horseshoe crabs, and has the longest known prey list of any sea turtle.

population.note: No global total in the source. Oman alone hosts around 15,000 nests.

citations.note: Oceans and seas the article names, plus countries with major nesting beaches (south-eastern United States, Brazil, Oman, Greece, Turkey, Cyprus, Japan, Australia, Mozambique and South Africa). Cape Verde is too small for our map.

media.altText: A loggerhead sea turtle swimming

editorial.overview: The only modern lizard that forages in the sea. It lives only on the Galápagos Islands of Ecuador, basking on black lava shores and diving for algae. Adults can shrink when food runs short during El Niño years. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Almost only red and green algae, grazed in the intertidal zone and under water.

population.note: No total in the source; it is locally abundant on some shores.

citations.note: Coasts of the Galápagos Islands, Ecuador.

media.altText: A marine iguana feeding on algae under water

editorial.overview: A yellow-green to bright gold toad, some with black spots, that is a national symbol of Panama and lived along mountain streams. The fungal disease chytridiomycosis wiped out the known wild populations; it may have been extinct in the wild since 2007 and survives in captive breeding programmes. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Tadpoles feed on algae while they develop over 6 to 7 months. The source does not describe what adults eat.

population.note: No wild population is known; it may have been extinct in the wild since 2007.

citations.note: Endemic to Panama, along streams on the eastern side of the Tabasará range (Coclé and Panamá provinces). Possibly extinct in the wild.

media.altText: A Panamanian golden frog

editorial.overview: A large, fully aquatic frog with baggy, wrinkled skin that lets it breathe through the skin in the cold, high-altitude water of the Lake Titicaca basin. It has an extremely low metabolic rate. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mostly amphipods and snails, plus insects and tadpoles; adults also eat small fish, and large frogs sometimes eat smaller ones.

population.note: No total in the source; it has declined drastically, and mass die-offs (thousands in 2015, about 10,000 in 2016) were recorded.

citations.note: Only in the Lake Titicaca basin, including its inflowing rivers and smaller connected lakes, in the Andes of Bolivia and Peru.

media.altText: A Titicaca water frog

editorial.overview: The largest ray in the world, found in tropical and temperate seas worldwide. It spends most of its life far from land, following currents to places where upwelling brings plankton. Females usually have a single pup after a long pregnancy, so populations recover slowly. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A filter feeder on zooplankton, which it gathers where nutrient-rich upwellings make plankton plentiful.

citations.note: Circumglobal in tropical and temperate waters, recorded from southern California, New Jersey and Japan in the north to Peru, Uruguay, South Africa and New Zealand in the south.

media.altText: A giant manta ray swimming above a diver

editorial.overview: The largest of all wrasses. It lives on coral reefs of the Indo-Pacific and the western Indian Ocean. Some recent sources place it in the genus Crassilabrus. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A top reef predator of invertebrates such as snails, clams, sea urchins and crustaceans, and of other fish. It even eats toxic animals such as sea hares and boxfish, and the coral-eating crown-of-thorns starfish.

population.note: No total in the source; numbers declined from the live reef food-fish trade.

citations.note: Coral reefs of the Indo-Pacific, from the east coast of Africa and the mouth of the Red Sea through parts of the Indian and Pacific oceans.

media.altText: A humphead wrasse on a coral reef

editorial.overview: A deep-blue, lobe-finned fish, first recognised by science from a specimen collected in South Africa in 1938. By day it rests in underwater caves, mostly 70 to 140 m deep, and it drifts out to hunt at night. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Hunts other fish and prey it finds in crevices; it has been seen doing "headstands" to slurp prey from cracks in lava caves.

population.note: No global total in the source; it says at most 370 individuals live off Grand Comoro.

citations.note: Sparse colonies around the rim of the western Indian Ocean, from South Africa north to Tanzania and Kenya, and around Madagascar and the Comoros (too small for our map).

media.altText: A coelacanth swimming near the sea floor

editorial.overview: The largest butterfly in the world: females can span more than 25 cm. It lives only in about 100 km² of coastal rainforest in Oro Province, Papua New Guinea, where it needs old-growth forest. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Caterpillars first eat their own eggshell, then feed on pipevines of the genus Pararistolochia, plants that contain aristolochic acids. Adults have few predators.

population.note: No total in the source; it is locally abundant within its tiny range.

citations.note: About 100 km² of coastal rainforest near Popondetta, Oro Province, Papua New Guinea.

media.altText: A pinned museum specimen of a male Queen Alexandra's birdwing

editorial.overview: A tree-dwelling tarantula and the only blue species of its genus. In the wild it is known only from one small, disturbed reserve forest in Andhra Pradesh, India. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly flying insects.

population.note: Population size is unknown according to the source.

citations.note: Less than 100 km² of deciduous reserve forest in Andhra Pradesh, southern India.

media.altText: A peacock tarantula

editorial.overview: A large freshwater mussel of clean, fast-flowing rivers on both sides of the North Atlantic. It grows extremely slowly and can live for more than two centuries. Its larvae must spend a stage on the gills of salmon or trout, so it depends on healthy fish populations. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A filter feeder: it draws water in through its siphons and filters out tiny organic particles.

population.note: No global total in the source; it gives figures for some countries (for example about 70,000 in two Austrian regions).

citations.note: Countries in the article's distribution list, from eastern Canada and New England through Europe to western Russia. Many of these populations are small or declining. Its "prey decline" here means the loss of the salmon and trout its larvae need.

media.altText: Outside and inside of a freshwater pearl mussel shell (museum specimen)

editorial.overview: A stony coral of the Caribbean and western Atlantic that grows in finger-like pillars, which can reach 3 m but are usually much smaller. It is the only species in its genus. Few young colonies survive, and it is very sensitive to bleaching and coral diseases. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Its polyps are among the few hard-coral polyps that can often be seen feeding during the day. The source does not say what it eats.

population.note: No colony count in the source.

citations.note: Warmer waters of the western Atlantic and the Caribbean, with many colonies in the Bahamas and off northern Jamaica. Functionally extinct in Florida. Apparently absent from Bermuda and the coasts of Panama and Colombia.

editorial.overview: The largest freshwater invertebrate and the largest freshwater crayfish in the world. It lives only in rivers and streams of northern Tasmania and needs cool, clean, well-oxygenated water with deep pools and fallen logs. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly decaying wood and leaves with the microbes on them; it also eats small fish, insects and rotting flesh when it can.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Experts estimate fewer than 100,000 remain in the wild.

citations.note: Rivers and streams of northern Tasmania, Australia, mostly 20 to 300 m above sea level.

editorial.overview: A large, snow-white crane with black wing feathers, a black neck in males and a patch of bare red skin on the crown, among the rarest cranes in the world. A migratory population breeds in Russia, China and Mongolia; a resident population lives in Hokkaido, Japan. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Highly omnivorous: rice, corn, buckwheat, grasses, berries, acorns and water plants such as reeds, as well as fish, amphibians and other small animals.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Winter counts in 2020 recorded more than 3,800 birds (adults and immatures), about 1,900 of them in Japan.

citations.note: Breeds in the Russian Far East, north-east China and occasionally north-eastern Mongolia, centred on Lake Khanka; winters on the Korean Peninsula and in east-central China. Resident in Hokkaido, Japan. Korea is not shown, because the source does not say which part of the peninsula.

editorial.overview: A large ray with a long, toothed "saw" on its snout, found in tropical and subtropical coasts and rivers, sometimes more than 1,000 km from the sea. Once plentiful, it has been wiped out from many regions. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Fish, molluscs and crustaceans. It uses its saw to stir up the bottom and to slash at groups of fish.

citations.note: Partial list of places where the article says it survives: northern Australia (the healthiest population), Papua New Guinea, the Amazon estuary in Brazil, Lake Nicaragua and the San Juan River, and off Colombia. Also in very low numbers off East Africa and the Indian subcontinent.
